engine_rules.name: Prefer string set with greatest vibrating length
engine_rules.falsifier: A chord voicing where the lower-string option produces unacceptable mechanical awkwardness or a clashing open string — in that case mechanical efficiency overrides sustain preference.
engine_rules.anchor: the musical quality can be enhanced by choosing a fingering or a set of strings in which the greater string length is maintained, thus permitting the Strings to "sing" and sustain longer

engine_rules.name: Eliminate unnecessary or awkward hand/finger movements
engine_rules.falsifier: A passage requiring a radical position jump for musical contrast — the jump is legitimate even though it violates the efficiency heuristic.
engine_rules.anchor: Mechanical efficiency is primarily a matter of avoiding unnecessary or awkward hand or finger movements

engine_rules.name: Open Voicing via Octave Displacement

then.octave.shift: move one or more chordal tones up or down one octave

engine_rules.falsifier: A voicing widened by interval adjustment other than octave displacement does not satisfy this technique
engine_rules.anchor: Closed voiced chords can be opened up as far as your reach will permit, simply by moving one or more chordal tones up or down an octave.

engine_rules.name: Counter Line Default String Placement
engine_rules.falsifier: A counter line placed in the bass voice or top melody voice does not follow this guideline
engine_rules.anchor: on guitar, are frequently found in the second voice from the top

engine_rules.name: Counter Line Activity Inversely Related to Melody Motion

then.voicing.shape: activate counter line with more motion

engine_rules.falsifier: A static counter line under a static melody does not apply this rule; an active counter line under an active melody contradicts it
engine_rules.anchor: When the main melody has little motion, the counter line can be more active.

engine_rules.name: Change Voicing or Inversion with Each Melody Note

then.voicing.strings: move chordal tones in same direction as melody where possible

engine_rules.falsifier: Holding the same chord form while the melody changes destroys the block chord effect
engine_rules.anchor: it is more desirable to change the voicing or inversion with each new melody note, in order to create the effect of all lines moving at once.

engine_rules.name: Gm7 as Substitute for Ebmaj9
engine_rules.falsifier: Substituting a chord with no shared tones with Ebmaj9 would not satisfy this specific substitution
engine_rules.anchor: The Gm7 in bar 3 is being used as a substitute for Eb maj 9.

engine_rules.name: Drop Chord Tones When Fingering Requires; Sustain as Long as Possible

then.voicing.shape: drop one or more chordal tones as needed
then.voicing.selection_order: sustain each chordal tone for as long as possible before dropping

engine_rules.falsifier: Dropping a tone immediately without sustaining it first prevents listener memory from registering it
engine_rules.anchor: if each chordal tone is sustained for as long as possible, the listener usually remember those notes that have been dropped.

_provenance.section_title: Sustained Chord Background and Dropped Tones

engine_rules.name: Short Punctuations Must Be Authoritative and Well-Placed to Maintain Harmonic Continuity

then.voicing.shape: short chord punctuation played with authority
then.voicing.selection_order: prefer voicings that emphasize chordal tones in melody

engine_rules.falsifier: A weakly articulated or poorly timed punctuation fails to outline harmonic flow and breaks continuity
engine_rules.anchor: These can be used without sacrificing harmonic continuity, when they are played with authority and appropriately placed within the bar.

engine_rules.name: Close Voicing as Texture Contrast
engine_rules.falsifier: If the preceding passage is already close-voiced, switching to close voicing provides no contrast and the rule does not apply.
engine_rules.anchor: close voicings, very effective but not too often used, on the guitar. These can be used as texture contrast to the big sound of open voicings

engine_rules.name: G6 as Eb7b9 Dominant Substitute
engine_rules.falsifier: G6 in a tonic or pre-dominant context (e.g., I6 in G major with no dominant pull toward Eb) does not function as Eb7b9.
engine_rules.anchor: The G6 in bar 3 is functioning as a dominant chord (Eb + 7b9)

_provenance.section_title: G6 Functioning as Dominant Chord (Eb7b9 Sub)

engine_rules.name: Diminished 7 Substitution for Dom7b9
engine_rules.falsifier: Diminished chord used as a passing chord between two diatonic chords (e.g., I° between I and ii) is not functioning as a dom7b9 substitute and this rule does not apply.
engine_rules.anchor: The E° and Dbo chords are both functioning as A7b9, and are being used to provide some chromatic relief from the monotony of diatonic lines

_provenance.section_title: Diminished Chords as Chromatic Dominant Substitution

engine_rules.name: Sustain Each Chord Tone for Maximum Duration
engine_rules.falsifier: A chord requiring a full position shift where no notes are common between successive chords — in that case no tones can be physically sustained across the change.
engine_rules.anchor: Sustain each chordal tone for as long as possible. In general. this means to keep your fingers in place until it's absolutely necessary to move them. This will contribute measurably to the continuity of your chord melody style

engine_rules.name: Two-Note Dyad as Implied Harmony
engine_rules.falsifier: When full block-chord texture is required (e.g., a sustained chord background), a two-note dyad fails to fill the harmonic space and the rule does not apply.
engine_rules.anchor: The use of two notes to create the overall effect of harmony has been Telativels unexplored in guitar playing, particularly in improvisation, and could, with practice, make a valuable contribution to the versatility of one's style

engine_rules.name: m7+5 Chromatic Passing Chord Between Diatonic Chords
engine_rules.falsifier: If the diatonic chords are a whole step apart and a half-step passing chord would land on another diatonic chord, the chromatic passing function is absorbed and a different passing quality may be required.
engine_rules.anchor: Example 35 shows the primary progression consisting of G6, Am7, Bm7, Cmaj 7 (one chord per bart being connected by the passing chords G#m7+5, Am7+5, et

_provenance.section_title: Chromatic Passing Chords Connecting Diatonic Progression

engine_rules.name: Develop Passing Tones into Counter Line and Melodic Pattern
engine_rules.falsifier: A single isolated passing tone that resolves immediately and has no continuation cannot be developed into a counter line without forcing artificial melodic material.
engine_rules.anchor: Example 37 shows further development of a counter line resulting from the extension of the passing tones into a more melodic pattern

_provenance.section_title: Counter Line Development into Melodic Pattern

engine_rules.name: Melody Register Voicing Constraint
engine_rules.falsifier: A satisfactory full chord voicing is found beneath a melody note on string 5 or 6 — which would contradict the constraint.
engine_rules.anchor: if the melody note is placed too low on the staff, you will not have enough strings left to form a satisfactory chord beneath it.

_provenance.section_title: Melody Register and Physical Voicing Constraints

engine_rules.name: 4th String Absolute Floor for Melody
engine_rules.anchor: It is possible however to play a low register scale or melody (as low as the 4th string but no lower) with some fragment of the chord beneath.

_provenance.section_title: Melody Register and Physical Voicing Constraints

engine_rules.name: Jumping Octaves When Melody Too Low
engine_rules.falsifier: Melodic continuity is lost when jumping octave — contradicts 'without losing melodic continuity' claim
engine_rules.anchor: you will often find it both helpful and necessary to transpose the melody up an octave (this is called "jumping octaves") several times throughout the course of a solo. With experience and finesse, this can be done without losing melodic continuity.

_provenance.section_title: Melody Register and Physical Voicing Constraints

engine_rules.name: Extensions Are Coloristic — Function Unchanged
engine_rules.falsifier: Adding maj7/6/9 to a chord changes its diatonic role or resolution behavior in the progression
engine_rules.anchor: the addition of the extensions Maj. 7th, 6th, 9th, etc., only affect the color and texture of the chord and do not change its scale function or its role in the progression

engine_rules.name: Any Chromatic Melody Note Is Harmonizable
engine_rules.falsifier: A chromatic melody note within finger range cannot be harmonized against any chord form — it must be avoided or the chord must change.
engine_rules.anchor: Any chromatic note within finger range can always be harmonized with a given chord form, although it may occasionally be dissonant.

engine_rules.name: Independent Melody and Harmony Voices Yield Extension Colors
engine_rules.falsifier: Independent melody/harmony motion produces no interesting extensions — all results are purely consonant triadic.
engine_rules.anchor: In each case the melody and the harmony have their own force and are independent of each other. Note the interesting extensions that occur as a result of this independence.
